title: Welcome: Course Map and Table of Contents
summary: See the whole 5-week course at a glance: every week, every unit, what you will be able to do, how the final assessment works and what you need beside you.

p: This course helps you teach Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language (0510) with confidence. It is written in simple words. You do not need to be an expert. You need to care about your students and be ready to practise.

Over five weeks you will move from the big picture to the classroom. First you learn the syllabus and the exam. Then you learn how the papers are marked. Next you plan the year. After that you plan lessons. Last you learn how to teach actively and make your own materials.
What you will be able to do at the end:
• Explain the aims, content, papers and marks of the 0510 syllabus.
• Mark reading, writing, listening and speaking work the way Cambridge examiners do.
• Plan a year, a module and a lesson that match the syllabus.
• Write a four-column scheme of work and a 50 to 60 minute lesson plan.
• Teach in a way that gives your students more time to talk.
• Make reading, writing and speaking tasks in the Cambridge style.
• Help students check their own progress with simple checklists.

b: Teachers who are new to Cambridge and want a clear start.
Experienced teachers who want to improve exam results.
Heads of department who train and support other teachers.
Anyone who prepares students for the IGCSE ESL exam.

sections.h: Table of contents: Week 1, Introductions and the syllabus
p: Week 1 gives you the foundations. It covers everything in the syllabus introduction and overview. It also gives you the Cambridge curriculum guide for school leaders. Nine units, about 8 hours.
• Unit 1: Welcome, course map and table of contents (this unit).
• Unit 2: Introductions I. Why choose this syllabus, before you start, entry dates, making entries, and your first two weeks with a new group.

• Unit 3: Implementing the Cambridge Curriculum. What a curriculum is, twelve principles of a good curriculum, the Cambridge Pathway, timetabling, the Cambridge teacher and learner, and an action plan. Includes the pathway picture.
• Unit 4: Introductions II. Accessibility and equality, access arrangements, after the exam, grades and how students and teachers use them.
• Unit 5: Syllabus overview. Aims, content, assessment overview, the sixteen assessment objectives and what they mean in class.
• Unit 6: Subject content. Reading, writing, listening and speaking, text types, phrase banks and teaching vocabulary and grammar.
• Unit 7: Details of the assessment. Paper 1, Paper 2 and Paper 3, exercise by exercise, plus the 2024 specimen paper.
• Unit 8: Planning your two-year programme. Syllabus to scheme of work, a sample outline, mock exams and tracking progress.
• Unit 9: Becoming a Cambridge educator. Support, training and professional habits.

b: You can describe every paper, how long it lasts and what it is worth.
You know how entries, access arrangements and grades work.
You have a rough plan for two years.

sections.h: Table of contents: Week 2, Assessment and marking
p: Week 2 teaches you to mark like a Cambridge examiner. You learn what the mark scheme says, what students get wrong and how to use past papers, the examiner reports and the specimen paper. Seven units, about 6 to 7 hours.
• Unit 10: Assessing the syllabus. How marks are awarded, the six generic marking principles, reading the mark scheme and best fit.
• Unit 11: Marking Paper 3 Speaking. How to run, record and mark the test, plus the teacher's notes for June 2024 and what the examiner report says about marking.
• Unit 12: Marking Exercises 1 and 3. Short answers and notes, with real student answers and examiner comments.
• Unit 13: Marking Exercises 2 and 4. Matching and multiple choice, and the hard questions.
• Unit 14: Marking Exercises 5 and 6. Content and Language tables, sample marking, and extra practice from the 2024 specimen paper.
• Unit 15: Paper 2 Listening, past papers and the examiner's report. Answer keys, lessons and a department plan.
• Unit 16: Standardising marking, giving feedback and improving results.

b: You can mark Paper 1 and Paper 3 fairly and in the same way as a colleague.
You can turn an examiner report into a teaching plan.
You have a marking portfolio.

sections.h: Table of contents: Week 3, Planning the journey
p: Week 3 moves from marking to planning. You build a year map, write a scheme of work, check what your students already know and start your learning tracker. Five units, about 4 hours.
• Unit 17: Long-term planning. The academic year map, real teaching time and the exam buffer.
• Unit 18: Medium-term planning. Writing a scheme of work with learning targets and assessment inside the module.
• Unit 19: Prerequisite knowledge. The four baseline skills and how to bridge gaps.
• Unit 20: Initial assessment. Build and use a 30-minute diagnostic test.
• Unit 21: My learning tracker. Update your KWL chart.

b: You have a year map with an exam buffer.
You have a four-column scheme of work for one theme.
You have a diagnostic test and a plan to use the results.

sections.h: Table of contents: Week 4, Using the scheme of work and preparing lessons
p: Week 4 brings you into the classroom. You turn the scheme of work into a lesson, week after week. Seven units, about 6 hours.
• Unit 22: From scheme of work to daily lesson. How the scheme of work and the lesson plan fit together.
• Unit 23: The four-column scheme of work in practice. Timeline and objectives, core tasks and skills, resources and technology, assessment methods. A worked two-week example.
• Unit 24: Lesson micro-structure. A 50 to 60 minute lesson with a starter, main interactive phases and a plenary. Timings, a template and a full sample lesson.
• Unit 25: Starters, plenaries and checks. Twelve starters, ten plenaries and exit tickets.
• Unit 26: Integrating skills. How reading and listening lead into writing and speaking in one sequence, with worked examples.
• Unit 27: Teaching with past papers and the specimen paper. Lesson sequences for each exercise.
• Unit 28: My learning tracker. Update your KWL chart and plan Week 5.

b: You can write a full lesson plan in 20 minutes.
You can link receptive skills to productive skills in one sequence.
You can use a past paper in a lesson without it turning into a test.

sections.h: Table of contents: Week 5, Teaching approaches and creating resources
p: Week 5 is about how you teach and what you teach with. You learn how to get your students talking, how to make your own tasks and how to help students check their own work. Eight units, about 8 hours.
• Unit 29: Communicative language teaching (CLT). What it is, how to give students more talking time, activity types and error correction.
• Unit 30: Task-based learning (TBL). The Willis framework, a full TBL lesson, and TBL compared with PPP.
• Unit 31: Teaching speaking for Paper 3. Using the teacher's notes and examiner report, timed practice, linking words and tenses.
• Unit 32: Creating reading worksheets. Turn real texts into Cambridge-style tasks for Exercises 1 to 4, with a worked example.
• Unit 33: Creating speaking and writing prompts. Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3 speaking cards, and writing tasks for Exercises 5 and 6.
• Unit 34: Adapting endorsed materials. How to scaffold or extend textbook exercises safely, and how to use publishers' books well.
• Unit 35: Formative checkpoints. Student-friendly peer and self-assessment checklists from the Cambridge criteria.
• Unit 36: Course wrap-up. Your learning tracker, action plan and how to prepare for the final assessment.

b: You have made at least three new tasks and tried one in class.
You have a set of checklists your students can use.
You have a 90-day action plan.

p: There is one final assessment. It has {{QCOUNT}} questions. It covers all five weeks. You need 75 percent to pass and earn your certificate.
The practice questions at the end of each unit do not count. They help you check your learning, and they unlock the final assessment when you finish.
What to expect:
• Questions on the syllabus, the papers and the mark schemes.
• Questions on marking and on the examiner reports.
• Questions about planning, lessons and teaching methods.
• Short real-life classroom situations where you choose the best action.

b: Read the key words at the top of each unit.
Do the 'Try it yourself' activity in each unit.
Review the practice questions you got wrong.
Keep your notes and templates in one folder.

p: Every unit uses the same pattern, so you always know what to expect.
• Short explanations in simple words, with key terms defined.
• Bullet points for the main ideas.
• Examples from real exam papers and real classrooms.
• Templates and checklists you can copy.
• A 'Try it yourself' activity for your own class.
• Three practice questions at the end.
How to study:
• Read one section at a time. Stop and think about your own students.
• Do the activity before you start the next unit.
• Study with a colleague if you can. Talk about the examples.
• Keep a notebook or a document with your plans, templates and ideas.

b: Day 1 to 2: read the units.
Day 3 to 4: do the activities with your class.
Day 5: update your KWL chart and note what you will change.

p: Collect these before you start. They are free or low cost. The course gives you downloads for many of them in the course materials box on the course page.
• The 0510 syllabus for 2024 to 2026 (download).
• The June 2024 Paper 1 question paper and mark scheme (download).
• The June 2024 Paper 2 mark scheme and audio (download).
• The 2024 specimen Paper 1 and its mark scheme (download).

• The Paper 3 Speaking teacher's notes with the speaking assessments. These are confidential, so they are not offered as a download here. Get them from your Cambridge account or exam officer and keep them secure. See Units 11 and 31.
• The June 2024 examiner report for teachers (download).
• The Cambridge guide for school leaders, Implementing the Curriculum with Cambridge (download).
Useful extras:

• A student's book that Cambridge endorses for the current syllabus. For example, the Collins Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language Student's Book, third edition, is endorsed for examination from 2024. Check the current list of endorsed resources on the Cambridge website before you buy.
• Access to the Cambridge School Support Hub. Your school's School Support Coordinator can set up an account. Look in the Teaching and learning section of the syllabus page.
• A phone or voice recorder, and a timer.
• Pens, sticky notes and large paper for group tasks.

b: Start with the syllabus and one past paper. You can do most of the course with those.
Ask your head of department which resources the school already has.
Use free online dictionaries and recorders for speaking practice.

activity: Print or copy the table of contents. Tick each unit as you finish it. Write your own aim for the five weeks in one sentence, and share it with a colleague.
